record_type_quote:
In Study 2, we conceptually replicated the studies of Braithwaite and Siegler (2018). That is,

we assessed whether Swiss sixth graders learned associations between operand features

and operations from rational arithmetic problems in their textbooks. Thus, this conceptual

replication tests the associative learning hypothesis in a different curricular context

(Switzerland).

targets.authors: Braithwaite, D. W., & Siegler, R. S.
targets.title: Children learn spurious associations in their math textbooks: Examples from fraction arithmetic.
targets.evidence_quote:
In Study 2, we conceptually replicated the studies of Braithwaite and Siegler (2018). That is,

we assessed whether Swiss sixth graders learned associations between operand features

and operations from rational arithmetic problems in their textbooks. Thus, this conceptual

replication tests the associative learning hypothesis in a different curricular context

(Switzerland).
targets.outcome_quote:
Thus, there are clearly nonrandom and unbalanced relations between arithmetic operations

and features of operands in the textbooks, however, slightly different from the results

presented by Braithwaite and Siegler (2018). Compared to U.S. textbooks, which included

addition and subtraction problems with equal- and unequal-denominator fractions at roughly

similar rates, Swiss textbooks show a striking imbalance: addition and subtraction problems

overwhelmingly involve unequal denominators, while equal-denominator cases are rare.
targets.outcome_reasoning: The authors confirm nonrandom distributions and learning of associations, but explicitly contrast the fraction operand distribution with the original. Aggregating the two retests gives mixed.

targets.authors: Tian, J., Braithwaite, D. W., & Siegler, R. S.
targets.title: Distributions of textbook tasks predict student learning: Data from decimal arithmetic.
targets.evidence_quote:
Our goal was to check whether Swiss

mathematics textbook series may also reveal imbalances in problem frequencies, as

reported by Braithwaite and Siegler (2018) and Tian et al. (2021) for U.S. textbooks.
targets.outcome_quote:
These patterns largely resemble, but differ also in part from those observed in U.S.

textbooks, analyzed by Braithwaite and Siegler (2018) and Tian et al. (2021). Most notably

(and to be explicitly tested in Study 2), in Swiss textbooks, children encounter +/- problems

involving fractions with unequal denominators more frequently than those involving equal

denominators. In contrast, U.S. textbooks present these two types of in roughly equal

proportions.
targets.outcome_reasoning: Study 1 confirms nonrandom decimal problem distributions but the authors also explicitly identify important distribution differences from the U.S. textbooks. The new child decimal tasks extend the finding rather than reproduce an original child experiment.

reasoning: Two Swiss textbook series and a new Swiss child sample retest published textbook-distribution and association findings. The computational model in Braithwaite et al. (2017) is not itself rerun. The discussion mentions Tian et al. (2022), but that paper concerns teacher assignment distributions, which this study does not test; the decimal textbook target is repeatedly and explicitly identified as Tian et al. (2021). Contrasts in tested textbook patterns accompany confirmation of the broad findings; no overall verdict erases those comparisons.
